steps.title: Identify the current sample in the supplied input
steps.prose: Read the input as seven chronological history samples followed by the new samples. a0 addresses the oldest history value. At the first output, array position seven is current; at the next output, the base slides one halfword and the current value is original position eight. Coefficients stay in oldest-first order, so the last stored coefficient multiplies the current sample.
steps.expectedObservation: One output requires eight input halfwords, two output bytes and the same sixteen coefficient bytes used by every output.

quiz.prompt: Which array position is current for output zero?

choices.text: Zero.
Seven.
Eight.

hints.text: Read the input as seven chronological history samples followed by the new samples.
One output requires eight input halfwords, two output bytes and the same sixteen coefficient bytes used by every output.

steps.title: Predict an asymmetric impulse response
steps.prose: First use the default impulse 16000 with all coefficients 4096: eight outputs are 2000 and later outputs zero. Then use impulse 16384 and unequal coefficients 1024,2048,3072,4096,5120,6144,7168,8192. The impulse enters at the current end and moves toward the oldest end in successive windows, exposing the stored coefficient order.
steps.expectedObservation: The unequal-coefficient response is 4096,3584,3072,2560,2048,1536,1024,512, then zeros.

quiz.prompt: Which stored coefficient determines the first impulse output?

choices.text: The last coefficient, position seven.
The first coefficient, position zero.
The sum of every coefficient regardless of impulse position.

hints.text: First use the default impulse 16000 with all coefficients 4096: eight outputs are 2000 and later outputs zero.
The unequal-coefficient response is 4096,3584,3072,2560,2048,1536,1024,512, then zeros.

steps.title: Inspect the two entries and provisional exits
steps.prose: The starter’s public fir_q15 entry tail-transfers to fir_scalar with an ordinary branch, preserving the caller’s ra. Complete the scalar function first. Its provided entry retains count and clears the per-call clipping total; its provided exit returns through ra. Each marked unfinished scalar region returns provisionally. Vector regions remain unreachable until the later entry edit.
steps.expectedObservation: The untouched starter assembles and exits but fails final filtering. A provisional return reports only the construction reached so far.

quiz.prompt: Does the initial transfer require a nested-call return address?

choices.text: Only for count zero.
Yes; every label transition changes ra.
No; the branch preserves the original caller continuation.

hints.text: The starter’s public fir_q15 entry tail-transfers to fir_scalar with an ordinary branch, preserving the caller’s ra.
The untouched starter assembles and exits but fails final filtering. A provisional return reports only the construction reached so far.

steps.title: Guard the output count before reading history
steps.prose: The public entry initially transfers directly to fir_scalar without changing ra. The scalar entry retains the requested count in v0 and clears v1. Test a3 before setting up any input or coefficient load. Seven history samples describe the input layout; they do not authorize an empty-output call to inspect caller data. Return through scalar_return when count is zero.
steps.expectedObservation: The zero-output recipe returns v0=0 and v1=0 without a caller-data read or write.

quiz.prompt: May an empty call load the coefficients merely because their sixteen bytes exist?

choices.text: No; the zero-output contract forbids caller-data access.
Yes; coefficients are always read-only.
Only when the history is zero.

hints.text: The public entry initially transfers directly to fir_scalar without changing ra.
The zero-output recipe returns v0=0 and v1=0 without a caller-data read or write.

steps.title: Start one complete eight-tap window
steps.prose: Clear t0 for the exact sum, copy the outer input address into t1 and the coefficient address into t2, then set the tap count in t3 to eight. The outer input address identifies this output window. Its private walker will traverse eight samples while the outer address stays in place until the output is stored. Coefficients restart from their base for every scalar output.
steps.expectedObservation: Before the first tap, t0=0 and t3=8. The two walkers identify the selected input and coefficient starts.

quiz.prompt: Which address should advance only once per output?

choices.text: The coefficient base after every output.
The caller’s return address.
The outer window base a0.

hints.text: Clear t0 for the exact sum, copy the outer input address into t1 and the coefficient address into t2, then set the tap count in t3 to eight.
Before the first tap, t0=0 and t3=8. The two walkers identify the selected input and coefficient starts.

steps.title: Load the oldest sample in this window
steps.prose: Use two unsigned byte loads from t1. The first tap sees the oldest history sample, not the first current sample at window position seven. Arbitrary byte alignment makes byte loads a direct way to respect the two-byte sample boundary. t4 and t5 still hold separate byte values; their combination and sign interpretation follow in separate edits.
steps.expectedObservation: For sample -1000, t4=24 and t5=252, the stored hexadecimal bytes 18 fc.

quiz.prompt: Which sample does tap zero multiply?

choices.text: The oldest sample of the selected window.
The sample after the window.
The first new sample regardless of window position.

hints.text: Use two unsigned byte loads from t1.
For sample -1000, t4=24 and t5=252, the stored hexadecimal bytes 18 fc.

steps.title: Join the sample’s low and high bytes
steps.prose: Shift the high byte left by eight and OR it into the low byte. These fields occupy disjoint bit positions, so this reconstructs low+256*high. The unsigned pattern is now complete in t4. The input address has not advanced, and bit fifteen has not yet been extended into the register’s higher positions.
steps.expectedObservation: The worked negative sample has unsigned halfword pattern 64536 in t4.

quiz.prompt: What has the OR produced?

choices.text: An input address advanced by eight.
The unsigned sixteen-bit sample pattern.
A complete weighted product.

hints.text: Shift the high byte left by eight and OR it into the low byte.
The worked negative sample has unsigned halfword pattern 64536 in t4.

steps.title: Extend the sample before multiplication
steps.prose: Use seh so the halfword sign bit determines the complete signed register value. The pattern fc18 must become -1000 rather than positive 64536. A correct coefficient cannot repair an unsigned interpretation of the sample. This representation step precedes every product, including products in later windows.
steps.expectedObservation: t4 is -1000 for the negative recipe and 32767 for the positive boundary recipe.

quiz.prompt: Which bit supplies the extension?

choices.text: Bit fifteen of the reconstructed sample.
The sign bit of the input address.
Bit seven of the low byte.

hints.text: Use seh so the halfword sign bit determines the complete signed register value.
t4 is -1000 for the negative recipe and 32767 for the positive boundary recipe.

steps.title: Load the matching Q15 coefficient
steps.prose: Read two bytes from t2 into t5 and t6. Reusing t5 is safe because the complete signed sample is retained in t4. This first coefficient multiplies the oldest sample. Its stored code supplies a weight only after the binary scale is applied to the complete dot product; the two loaded bytes are not separate weights.
steps.expectedObservation: Coefficient -16384 has low byte zero and high byte 192. The signed sample -1000 remains in t4.

quiz.prompt: Why may t5 be reused here?

choices.text: All coefficients are positive.
Loading a coefficient stores the sample automatically.
The signed sample no longer depends on its former high-byte temporary.

hints.text: Read two bytes from t2 into t5 and t6.
Coefficient -16384 has low byte zero and high byte 192. The signed sample -1000 remains in t4.

steps.title: Reconstruct the coefficient code
steps.prose: Shift t6 left by eight and combine it into t5. The stored order is the same little-endian order as the input samples. A Q15 scale does not change byte order or make the raw code unsigned. This edit recovers the numerical pattern; the next edit gives that pattern its signed interpretation.
steps.expectedObservation: Coefficient bytes 00 c0 reconstruct unsigned pattern 49152 in t5.

quiz.prompt: Does the Q15 scale reverse the stored bytes?

choices.text: Yes; fractional values use the high byte first.
Only for negative coefficients.
No; the contract still stores the low byte first.

hints.text: Shift t6 left by eight and combine it into t5.
Coefficient bytes 00 c0 reconstruct unsigned pattern 49152 in t5.

steps.title: Give the coefficient its signed value
steps.prose: Sign-extend the coefficient halfword with seh. Code c000 represents -16384, a weight of negative one half. Multiplying the same sample by a positive or negative weight must change the contribution’s sign as ordinary signed arithmetic requires. Keep the code as an integer; do not shift it down to an integral weight before multiplication.
steps.expectedObservation: t5 is -16384 in the negative-coefficient recipe and 16384 in the positive recipe.

quiz.prompt: Why not divide the coefficient by 32768 at this point?

choices.text: That would discard the fractional weight before the product.
The coefficient is already a full address.
Every coefficient represents an integer greater than one.

hints.text: Sign-extend the coefficient halfword with seh.
t5 is -16384 in the negative-coefficient recipe and 16384 in the positive recipe.

steps.title: Form the exact signed product
steps.prose: Multiply the two sign-extended values with dmul and retain the product in t7. The sample and coefficient are bounded signed halfwords, so their exact product fits this doubleword result. The accumulator remains separate in t0. Preserve the product’s low-scale bits for the final rounding; no per-product Q15 shift belongs here.
steps.expectedObservation: The worked product is 16384000. Two minimum codes produce 1073741824 for one product. The accumulator is still zero.

quiz.prompt: Which value still contains the pre-add accumulator?

hints.text: Multiply the two sign-extended values with dmul and retain the product in t7.
The worked product is 16384000. Two minimum codes produce 1073741824 for one product. The accumulator is still zero.

steps.title: Add the product without narrowing the sum
steps.prose: Add t7 into t0 using daddu. A single product fits a signed word, but a partial sum of two maximum positive products does not. Doubleword accumulation preserves every allowed partial sum. The tap count is still eight here because consuming a tap belongs to the next region, after its product has contributed.
steps.expectedObservation: The first worked contribution leaves t0=16384000 and t3=8.

quiz.prompt: Why use a doubleword addition even though one product fits a word?

choices.text: It makes rounding unnecessary.
It permits reading beyond the input window.
The complete and partial sums may exceed signed word range.

hints.text: Add t7 into t0 using daddu.
The first worked contribution leaves t0=16384000 and t3=8.

steps.title: Consume exactly eight matched pairs
steps.code:
daddiu $t1, $t1, 2
    daddiu $t2, $t2, 2
    addiu $t3, $t3, -1
    bne $t3, $zero, scalar_tap
    nop
steps.prose: Advance both private walkers by two, decrement t3 and repeat scalar_tap while a pair remains. The outer a0 window base stays unchanged. On the last pair, fall through to scalar_round. This completes an exact dot product; output storage is still unfinished. The coefficient walker must not keep its end position for the next output.
steps.expectedObservation: Eight minimum/minimum products leave exact t0=8589934592 and t3=0. Eight sample-one, half-weight products leave t0=131072. Both walkers advance sixteen bytes.

quiz.prompt: Where does the coefficient walker begin for the next output?

choices.text: At the unchanged coefficient base.
Sixteen bytes beyond the coefficient array.
At the destination byte after the last store.

hints.text: Advance both private walkers by two, decrement t3 and repeat scalar_tap while a pair remains.
Eight minimum/minimum products leave exact t0=8589934592 and t3=0. Eight sample-one, half-weight products leave t0=131072. Both walkers advance sixteen bytes.

steps.title: Add half a scale unit once
steps.prose: Add 16384 to the complete accumulator with daddiu. This is half of 32768 in accumulator units. It prepares one final nearest rounding with ties toward positive infinity. Adding the bias once per product would change the filter; the completed eight-tap loop must reach this region only after all products have accumulated.
steps.expectedObservation: Accumulators 16384, -16384 and -16385 become 32768, zero and -1 before shifting.

quiz.prompt: How many times is this bias added per output?

choices.text: Once for the entire multi-output call.
Once, after the full exact sum.
Once per tap.

hints.text: Add 16384 to the complete accumulator with daddiu.
Accumulators 16384, -16384 and -16385 become 32768, zero and -1 before shifting.

steps.title: Use an arithmetic shift for floor division
steps.prose: Shift t0 right arithmetically by fifteen with dsra. Together with the bias, this implements floor((S+16384)/32768). A negative biased value must round downward under the division, so truncation toward zero would be wrong. A logical shift would replace the sign with zeros and produce a large positive value.
steps.expectedObservation: The three tie-adjacent recipes produce rounded codes one, zero and -1. The maximum eight-product sum produces 262144 before saturation.

quiz.prompt: What does biased value -1 produce after this shift?

choices.text: Zero.

hints.text: Shift t0 right arithmetically by fifteen with dsra.
The three tie-adjacent recipes produce rounded codes one, zero and -1. The maximum eight-product sum produces 262144 before saturation.

steps.title: Test the rounded upper endpoint strictly
steps.prose: Compare rounded t0 with 32767 using a strict signed test. The filter’s clipping count concerns the rounded result, not the raw accumulator. Equality is representable and must pass to the lower test. A result larger than the endpoint goes to scalar_high, whose replacement is still unfinished.
steps.expectedObservation: Rounded 262144 takes the high path with t9=1. Constant maximum input under the moving average gives 32767 with t9=0.

quiz.prompt: Does an exact rounded endpoint count as clipped?

choices.text: Yes, whenever it equals 32767.
No.
Only when the coefficients sum to one.

hints.text: Compare rounded t0 with 32767 using a strict signed test.
Rounded 262144 takes the high path with t9=1. Constant maximum input under the moving average gives 32767 with t9=0.

steps.title: Keep rounded in-range values on the store path
steps.code:
li $t8, -32768
    slt $t9, $t0, $t8
    bne $t9, $zero, scalar_low
    nop
    beq $zero, $zero, scalar_store
    nop
steps.prose: Test whether the rounded result is smaller than -32768. Branch to scalar_low when it is; otherwise transfer directly to scalar_store. This bypasses both endpoint replacement and the clipping increment. An accumulator representing -32768.5 rounds to -32768 under this contract, so its clipping decision must use that rounded value.
steps.expectedObservation: Rounded -262136 takes the low path. Rounded -32768 and zero go to storage without increasing the count.

quiz.prompt: Which quantity determines clipping in this exercise?

choices.text: The sign of the first product.
The number of negative coefficients.
The complete rounded sample code.

hints.text: Test whether the rounded result is smaller than -32768.
Rounded -262136 takes the low path. Rounded -32768 and zero go to storage without increasing the count.

steps.title: Choose the positive endpoint
steps.prose: Load 32767 into t0, then transfer to the shared scalar_clipped label. The branch skips the negative endpoint replacement. Keep the clipping count separate from the stored endpoint: an ordinary in-range endpoint produces the same two bytes. At this partial stage, the replacement has happened but the counter region is still unfinished.
steps.expectedObservation: A large positive result becomes 32767 while v1 remains zero until the next count edit.

quiz.prompt: Why skip the following negative replacement?

choices.text: The return count is stored in the next label.
The two overflow directions need different endpoint values.
Both replacements must always execute.

hints.text: Load 32767 into t0, then transfer to the shared scalar_clipped label.
A large positive result becomes 32767 while v1 remains zero until the next count edit.

steps.title: Choose the negative endpoint
steps.prose: Load -32768 into t0 for the lower-overflow path. It falls through to scalar_clipped, sharing the increment with positive overflow. In-range flow already bypasses this path. The exact negative endpoint and a clipped negative result therefore remain distinguishable through their count even though their stored bytes agree.
steps.expectedObservation: A large negative rounded result becomes -32768 with v1 still zero at the next unfinished region.

quiz.prompt: Can the final endpoint bytes alone reveal whether this path executed?

choices.text: Only when output is word aligned.
Yes; negative endpoints are always clipped.
No.

hints.text: Load -32768 into t0 for the lower-overflow path.
A large negative rounded result becomes -32768 with v1 still zero at the next unfinished region.

steps.title: Count one replacement per output
steps.prose: Increment v1 at scalar_clipped. Either out-of-range direction reaches this label once; in-range flow goes directly to scalar_store. The entry initialized v1 for the call, so this edit accumulates events across outputs. It does not count clipped taps or changes to individual output bytes.
steps.expectedObservation: Large positive and negative results each contribute one; exact rounded endpoints contribute zero.

quiz.prompt: What unit does v1 count?

choices.text: Products outside halfword range.
Bytes written to the output.
Outputs whose rounded result needed saturation.

hints.text: Increment v1 at scalar_clipped.
Large positive and negative results each contribute one; exact rounded endpoints contribute zero.

steps.title: Write the first output byte only
steps.prose: Store the result’s low byte at a2 with sb. A halfword result occupies exactly two permitted bytes, even at an odd address. This first store publishes one byte and leaves the second poisoned byte untouched. Input and coefficients are immutable under this FIR contract, so no in-place assumption from the mixer may justify storing into either source.
steps.expectedObservation: Positive saturation writes ff as its first byte; negative saturation writes 00. The second byte remains a5.

quiz.prompt: Why would a word store violate this operation’s ownership?

choices.text: It reads the coefficient backwards.
It cannot represent a positive endpoint.
It changes bytes beyond the two-byte sample.

hints.text: Store the result’s low byte at a2 with sb.
Positive saturation writes ff as its first byte; negative saturation writes 00. The second byte remains a5.

steps.title: Complete the low-byte-first halfword
steps.prose: Shift the result right by eight into t1 and store that register’s low byte at a2+1. For a negative result, a logical shift is sufficient here because sb selects just the original bits fifteen through eight. This differs from the arithmetic shift used for signed rounding. The input/output window advance is still a separate operation.
steps.expectedObservation: Positive saturation stores ff 7f; negative saturation stores 00 80. Each overflow contributes one event.

quiz.prompt: Why can this byte-extraction shift be logical?

choices.text: It replaces the earlier rounding operation.
Only the next selected byte is stored.
Negative output codes have no high bits.

hints.text: Shift the result right by eight into t1 and store that register’s low byte at a2+1.
Positive saturation stores ff 7f; negative saturation stores 00 80. Each overflow contributes one event.

steps.title: Advance the outer input by one sample
steps.code:
daddiu $a0, $a0, 2
    daddiu $a2, $a2, 2
    addiu $a3, $a3, -1
    bne $a3, $zero, scalar_window
    nop
steps.prose: Advance a0 and a2 by two, consume one output and repeat scalar_window while count remains. The new input window overlaps seven samples of the previous window. Its private walkers and accumulator restart, while v1 keeps the call’s accumulated clipping count. The scalar path now implements every supported count, including asymmetric impulse responses and maximum sums.
steps.expectedObservation: The default sixteen-output impulse returns eight samples of 2000 then zeros. The asymmetric two-output fixture yields 4096 then 3584. Sixty-four maximum positive sums return sixty-four clipping events.

quiz.prompt: Why advance the input by two rather than sixteen bytes?

choices.text: Each next output slides the eight-tap window by one sample.
The window has only one input byte.
The coefficients advance automatically with a0.

hints.text: Advance a0 and a2 by two, consume one output and repeat scalar_window while count remains.

The default sixteen-output impulse returns eight samples of 2000 then zeros. The asymmetric two-output fixture yields 4096 then 3584. Sixty-four maximum positive sums return sixty-four clipping events.

steps.title: Inspect the provided vector quantizer before switching
steps.prose: The vector path already contains the rounding, bounds, endpoint replacement, counting and byte stores just developed in the scalar path. Compare its fir labels with their scalar counterparts. The final vector sum must arrive in t0; v0 retains the original count and v1 accumulates clipped outputs. Reusing the established rule avoids introducing a different quantizer while changing the dot product.
steps.expectedObservation: The vector postprocessing advances a0 by two, keeps the coefficient base, and repeats fir_window. It applies one bias and arithmetic shift after each complete sum.

quiz.prompt: What must the vector reduction supply to the provided postprocessing?

choices.text: One exact complete accumulator in t0.
Only the low word of a pair sum.
Eight separately rounded halfwords.

hints.text: The vector path already contains the rounding, bounds, endpoint replacement, counting and byte stores just developed in the scalar path.
The vector postprocessing advances a0 by two, keeps the coefficient base, and repeats fir_window. It applies one bias and arithmetic shift after each complete sum.

steps.title: Switch the public entry to the vector path
steps.prose: Replace the provisional tail transfer to fir_scalar with the real fir_q15 entry: retain count, clear v1 and return at zero before coefficient setup. The completed scalar routine remains available as a comparison. Positive calls now reach unfinished vector regions and return provisionally; that temporary state is not a correct filtered result yet.
steps.expectedObservation: Zero count returns without caller-data access. A one-output call reaches the unfinished coefficient load with v0=1, v1=0 and no output written.

quiz.prompt: Does switching the public entry remove the scalar comparison function?

choices.text: No; it remains available under fir_scalar.
Yes; its completed code must be discarded.
Only when the input history is zero.

hints.text: Replace the provisional tail transfer to fir_scalar with the real fir_q15 entry: retain count, clear v1 and return at zero before coefficient setup.
Zero count returns without caller-data access. A one-output call reaches the unfinished coefficient load with v0=1, v1=0 and no output written.

steps.title: Load the coefficient window once
steps.prose: Load all sixteen coefficient bytes into w1 before the output loop. Each nonempty output uses the same eight weights, so this setup is outside fir_window. The zero guard has already excluded empty calls. Byte loading does not require a halfword-aligned coefficient address in the pinned implementation.
steps.expectedObservation: w1 contains all eight coefficient codes in stored oldest-first order.

quiz.prompt: How many coefficient bytes does this load transfer?

choices.text: Two.
Eight.
Sixteen.

hints.text: Load all sixteen coefficient bytes into w1 before the output loop.
w1 contains all eight coefficient codes in stored oldest-first order.

steps.title: Build the coefficient sign-extension mask
steps.prose: Compare each signed halfword in w1 with zero. clti_s.h produces ffff where a coefficient is negative and zero otherwise. These bits will supply the high half of each word. A sign mask is a representation tool here; it does not count negative coefficients or change their scale.
steps.expectedObservation: For the mixed-sign recipe, mask lanes are ffff,0000,ffff,0000,ffff,0000,0000,0000.

quiz.prompt: Which halfwords must have an all-one high extension?

choices.text: The negative coefficients.
Only the coefficient at index seven.
Every coefficient with a nonzero low byte.

hints.text: Compare each signed halfword in w1 with zero.
For the mixed-sign recipe, mask lanes are ffff,0000,ffff,0000,ffff,0000,0000,0000.

steps.title: Widen the first four coefficient lanes
steps.prose: Interleave w1’s low halfwords with their corresponding mask halfwords into w3. Operand order makes each original code the low half of a word and its mask the high half. In little-endian interpretation this sign-extends the value. Zero extension would change a negative coefficient into a positive number before multiplication.
steps.expectedObservation: w3’s words represent -32768,32767,-16384,16384; their raw hexadecimal patterns retain full signed extensions.

quiz.prompt: Which word represents coefficient -32768 correctly?

choices.text: ffff8000.

hints.text: Interleave w1’s low halfwords with their corresponding mask halfwords into w3.
w3’s words represent -32768,32767,-16384,16384; their raw hexadecimal patterns retain full signed extensions.

steps.title: Retain the other four widened coefficients
steps.prose: Use the high interleave to place coefficient positions four through seven in w4. These words use the same sign-extension rule as the low half. Keep both w3 and w4 unchanged across output windows. The loop will rebuild input values and dot products without consuming the retained coefficient vectors.
steps.expectedObservation: w4’s signed words are -1,1,0,4096.

quiz.prompt: Which coefficient positions belong to this vector?

choices.text: Zero through three again.
Four through seven.
Eight through eleven.

hints.text: Use the high interleave to place coefficient positions four through seven in w4.
w4’s signed words are -1,1,0,4096.

steps.title: Load one complete eight-tap input window
steps.prose: Load sixteen bytes from a0 into w0 for this output. Even count one has eight input samples because its seven history samples precede the current sample. The load fits the logical input slice. After storage the outer loop advances by two, so subsequent loads intentionally overlap most of these bytes.
steps.expectedObservation: w0 holds the eight supplied sample codes, including history, in chronological order.

quiz.prompt: Does count one authorize this sixteen-byte load?

choices.text: Only if the destination is also the source.
No; eight outputs are required.
Yes; its input includes seven history samples and one current sample.

hints.text: Load sixteen bytes from a0 into w0 for this output.
w0 holds the eight supplied sample codes, including history, in chronological order.

steps.title: Derive a fresh sign mask for the window
steps.prose: Compare each signed sample halfword with zero into w2. The coefficient mask is no longer needed because its widened words are already retained. Reusing w2 is safe, but retaining the preceding output’s sample mask would not be: the new window can contain different signs at each position.
steps.expectedObservation: The mixed-sign input mask is ffff,0000,ffff,0000,ffff,0000,0000,0000.

quiz.prompt: Why recompute this mask each output?

choices.text: The coefficient scale changes each call.
The input window changes.
A mask must always contain the clipping count.

hints.text: Compare each signed sample halfword with zero into w2.
The mixed-sign input mask is ffff,0000,ffff,0000,ffff,0000,0000,0000.

steps.title: Widen the first four input samples
steps.prose: Interleave the low input halfwords with their sign masks into w5. The word values must remain the original signed sample codes; there is no Q15 scaling operation in this widening. Their correspondence with coefficient words in w3 establishes the first four products in the dot reduction.

quiz.prompt: Does widening multiply a sample by 65536?

choices.text: Yes; every new word shifts the code left.
Only for a negative sample.
No; correct sign extension preserves its numerical value.

hints.text: Interleave the low input halfwords with their sign masks into w5.

steps.title: Widen the final four input samples
steps.prose: Use the high interleave for sample positions four through seven, producing w6. Its word positions now match the retained high coefficient vector w4. The current sample is the last word of this vector, not the first. Both input halves are ready before either dot product runs.
steps.expectedObservation: w6’s signed words are -1,1,0,16000.

quiz.prompt: Where is the current sample in this window?

choices.text: Outside the loaded sixteen bytes.
At position seven, the last widened input word.
At position zero.

hints.text: Use the high interleave for sample positions four through seven, producing w6.
w6’s signed words are -1,1,0,16000.

steps.title: Form two exact doubleword pair sums
steps.prose: Apply dotp_s.d to the first four widened sample/coefficient words. Its two destination lanes sum products zero/one and two/three. The d suffix describes doubleword results; the multiplied inputs are signed words. In this bounded domain, both pair sums are exact, including positive 2147483648 that cannot be held as a signed word result.
steps.expectedObservation: The mixed-sign fixture gives 2147418113 and 32768000 in w7. Minimum/minimum pairs give 2147483648 in each doubleword.

quiz.prompt: Why not use dotp_s.w directly on the original halfwords?

choices.text: An allowed two-product sum can overflow its signed word result.
It would process no products.
It requires aligned output but otherwise gives the same exact sum.

hints.text: Apply dotp_s.d to the first four widened sample/coefficient words.
The mixed-sign fixture gives 2147418113 and 32768000 in w7. Minimum/minimum pairs give 2147483648 in each doubleword.

steps.title: Include the last four tap products
steps.prose: Apply dotp_s.d to w6 and w4, retaining pair sums for positions four/five and six/seven in w8. The current sample’s contribution is part of the latter pair. Matching input and coefficient halves matters; combining high samples with low coefficients would implement different weights even though every access stayed in bounds.
steps.expectedObservation: The mixed-sign fixture gives 2 and 65536000 in w8. The extreme fixture again gives two positive 2147483648 sums.

quiz.prompt: Which pair includes the current sample?

choices.text: Positions zero and one.
No pair; history alone determines output.
Positions six and seven.

hints.text: Apply dotp_s.d to w6 and w4, retaining pair sums for positions four/five and six/seven in w8.
The mixed-sign fixture gives 2 and 65536000 in w8. The extreme fixture again gives two positive 2147483648 sums.

steps.title: Combine the two halves without narrowing

steps.title: Distinguish rounding from a clipping event
steps.prose: Use the documented negative halfway accumulator -1073758208. It represents -32768.5 sample-code units but rounds toward positive infinity to -32768, which is representable. Compare it with a result that rounds to -32769. The clipping decision belongs after quantization, even when a raw accumulator lies beyond a scaled endpoint.
steps.expectedObservation: The halfway case returns the negative endpoint with zero clips; the rounded -32769 case returns the same endpoint with one clip.

quiz.prompt: Should raw value -32768.5 count as clipped under this contract?

choices.text: No; its rounded code is -32768.
